items.q: Child with otitis media now has postauricular swelling pushing the pinna forward and fever. Diagnosis?
items.exp: Pus coalescing in mastoid air cells with subperiosteal swelling displaces the pinna in mastoiditis, the commonest complication of acute otitis media needing imaging and surgical assessment.
r: Incorrect. Canal disease does not displace pinna from behind.
Correct. Postauricular swelling with pinna displacement is mastoiditis.
Incorrect. Wax stays in canal without fever swelling.
Incorrect. Perichondritis inflames pinna itself, sparing mastoid.
items.kp: Swelling behind ear pushing pinna out: mastoiditis.

items.q: Commonest intracranial complication of otitis media is which?
items.exp: Meningitis is the most frequent intracranial complication of otitis media, ahead of abscess and sinus thrombosis. Any ear infection with meningism needs urgent antibiotics and imaging guided puncture decisions.
r: Incorrect. Abscess is feared but less common than meningitis.
Correct. Meningitis is commonest intracranially.
Incorrect. Sinus thrombosis is rarer still.
Incorrect. Empyema is uncommon.
items.kp: Ear to meninges is the commonest deep escape.

items.q: Swinging picket fence fevers with rigors in chronic ear disease suggest what?
items.exp: Infected sigmoid sinus clot intermittently showers bacteria causing hectic picket fence rigors, with papilloedema from venous obstruction. Blood cultures taken during rigor grow the organism.
r: Incorrect. Labyrinthitis causes vertigo and deafness.
Correct. Hectic rigors mean infected sinus clot.
Incorrect. Simple mastoiditis gives steady local fever.
Incorrect. Palsy is motor, not septic pattern.
items.kp: Rigors like a picket fence: sinus clot seeding blood.

items.q: Otorrhoea, retro-orbital pain and abducens palsy together form which syndrome?
items.exp: Petrous apicitis inflames structures at the petrous tip: trigeminal pain behind the eye plus abducens palsy with ear discharge is Gradenigo syndrome, a mastoiditis complication variant.
r: Incorrect. Ramsay Hunt is facial palsy with vesicles.
Correct. Gradenigo triad at petrous apex.
Incorrect. Tolosa Hunt is painful ophthalmoplegia without ear disease.
Incorrect. Frey is gustatory sweating after parotid surgery.
items.kp: Ear discharge plus eye pain plus lateral gaze palsy: Gradenigo.

items.q: Otogenic brain abscess most characteristically lodges where?
items.exp: Contiguous spread through tegmen reaches temporal lobe, and via Trautmann triangle to cerebellum, so otogenic abscesses occupy these two sites. Frontal abscesses instead follow sinusitis.
r: Incorrect. Frontal abscess is classic for sinus source.
Correct. Temporal lobe and cerebellum for ear source.
Incorrect. Occipital lesions suggest haematogenous spread.
Incorrect. Brainstem abscess is rare and usually blood borne.
items.kp: Ear abscess: temporal lobe or cerebellum.

items.q: Facial palsy appearing with acute otitis media most often needs what principle?
o: Urgent ENT assessment; decompression considered with mastoid surgery
items.exp: The facial canal often dehisces in middle ear, so infection inflames or compresses the nerve. Urgent specialist care with antibiotics and possible surgical decompression or mastoid clearance protects recovery.
r: Incorrect. Delay worsens nerve outcome.
Correct. Urgent ENT care and source surgery assessment.
Incorrect. Steroids alone ignore infected source.
Incorrect. Exercises do not treat compression.
items.kp: Weak face with infected ear: urgent source control.

items.q: Bezold abscess is mastoid pus tracking where?
items.exp: Pus perforating the medial mastoid tip tracks deep to sternomastoid into the neck as Bezold abscess, presenting as neck swelling with torticollis in mastoiditis. It needs drainage with mastoid surgery.
r: Incorrect. Cheek swelling is dental or parotid source.
Correct. Neck tracking from mastoid tip is Bezold.
Incorrect. Orbit complications come from ethmoid sinuses.
Incorrect. Palatal swelling is dental or tonsillar.
items.kp: Mastoid tip pus in neck equals Bezold abscess.

items.q: Vertigo induced by pressure on the tragus in chronic ear disease indicates what?
items.exp: Cholesteatoma eroding the lateral canal lets pressure transmit to labyrinth, causing vertigo and nystagmus on tragus pressure: positive fistula sign needing urgent surgery planning without repeated pressure testing.
r: Incorrect. BPPV follows head position, not tragus pressure, without ear disease.
Correct. Pressure vertigo means labyrinth fistula.
Incorrect. Meniere has episodic vertigo with fluctuating hearing, no fistula.
Incorrect. Neuroma deafens slowly without pressure fistula signs.
items.kp: Press the ear, world spins: fistula present.

items.q: Before lumbar puncture in suspected otogenic brain abscess, what must happen?
o: Brain imaging to exclude mass effect
items.exp: Puncturing with abscess or raised intracranial pressure risks coning, so CT or MRI precedes lumbar puncture whenever focal signs, seizures or papilloedema exist. Cultures and antibiotics should not wait meanwhile per protocol.
r: Incorrect. Route matters less than herniation safety sequence.
Correct. Image first when abscess possible.
Incorrect. Mastoid films do not clear puncture safety.
Incorrect. Hearing tests never gate puncture.

items.q: Labyrinthitis complicating ear infection typically causes what hearing pattern?
items.exp: Infection or toxins entering inner ear destroy cochlear and vestibular function together: profound sensorineural deafness with violent vertigo, nausea and nystagmus. Serous forms may partly recover; suppurative usually not.
r: Incorrect. Inner ear injury is sensorineural, not conductive.
Correct. Sensorineural deafness plus severe vertigo.
Incorrect. Vertigo is defining, not absent.
Incorrect. Hearing loss is major, not spared.
items.kp: Deaf plus spinning after ear infection: labyrinth inflamed.
